pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Why is reading element 3,000,000 of an array exactly as cheap as reading element 3? And why is iterating an array faster in practice than its Big-O alone suggests?
expected_points: elements are contiguous, so address = base + index x element size — constant arithmetic, no walking
sequential iteration is cache-friendly: fetching one element pulls its neighbors into the cache line, and the hardware prefetches ahead

questions.prompt: Give me the Big-O of index, search, insert-at-head, and insert-at-tail — first for a slice, then for your linked list.
expected_points: slice: index O(1), search O(n), insert-at-head O(n) due to shifting, append amortized O(1)
list: index O(n), search O(n), insert-at-head O(1), insert-at-tail O(1) with a tail pointer (O(n) without)

questions.prompt: People say linked lists have O(1) insertion. What's the fine print on that claim?
expected_points: O(1) only when you already hold a reference to the node at the insertion point
finding that position is O(n), so search-then-insert is O(n) overall

questions.prompt: Workload A: build a lookup table once, then millions of reads by index. Workload B: a long queue-like buffer with constant removal at the front at large n. Which structure for each, and why?
expected_points: A: slice — O(1) indexing and cache-friendly memory, no shape changes after build
B: linked list becomes defensible — O(1) front removal versus O(n) shifting per removal on a slice
mentions the practical caveat: slices often still win at moderate n because of cache behavior and per-node memory overhead

questions.prompt: In your Delete you walked with both prev and cur. Why is prev unavoidable in a singly linked list, and which edge case did the tail pointer force you to handle?
expected_points: unlinking a node means rewriting the pointer aimed at it, which lives in the previous node — a singly linked node cannot reach its predecessor
deleting the last node must move tail back to prev, or a later Append attaches to an unlinked node

questions.prompt: A slice append sometimes copies the whole backing array. How can appending still be called O(1)?
expected_points: capacity roughly doubles on growth, so copies become geometrically rarer as the slice grows
total cost of n appends stays O(n), so the average per append is O(1) — that averaged accounting is what 'amortized' means
